questions.q: Mean of $n$ observations $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}$ is $\bar{x}$. If an observation $x_{q}$, is replaced by $x_q^{\prime}$ then the new mean is
questions.solution: We have, \bar{x}=$\frac{x_{1}+x_{2}+\ldots+x_{q}+\ldots+x_{2}}{n}\Rightarrow \quad \Sigma x=n \bar{x}$ If $x_{q}$, is replaced by $x_q^{\prime}$, then new total will be $\Sigma x'=\Sigma x-x_{4}-x_{4}^{\prime}$ New mean will be $\begin{array}{l} \barx^{\prime}=\frac{\Sigma x^{\prime}}{n}$\\ \barx^{\prime}=$\frac{\sum x-x_{q}+x_i^{\prime}}{n}$\\ \barx^{\prime}=$\frac{n \bar{x}-x_{q}+x_i^{\prime}}{n} \end{array}$

questions.q: Standard deviation of $n$ observations $a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}, \ldots, a_{n}$ is ${\sigma}.$ Then, the standard deviation of the observations $\lambda a_{1}, \lambda a_{2}, \ldots, \lambda a_{n}$ is
questions.solution: Let $x_{i}=a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}, \ldots, a_{n}$ and $y_{i}=\lambda a_{1}, \lambda a_{2}, \lambda a_{3}, \ldots, \lambda a_{n-}$ y_{i}=\lambda x_{i} $\because\begin{aligned} \bar{y} &=\frac{\Sigma y_{i}}{N} \\ &=\frac{\Sigma \lambda x_{i}}{n} \end{aligned} \begin{aligned}$&=\lambda $\frac{\Sigma x_{i}}{n}$\\ &=\lambda \bar{x} \\ \sigma_{y} &=$\sqrt{\frac{\Sigma\left(y_{i}-\bar{y}\right)^{2}}{N}}$\\ &=$\sqrt{\frac{\Sigma(\lambda x_{i}-\lambda \bar{x})^{2}}{n}}$\\ &=$\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{2} \Sigma\left(x_{i}-\bar{x}\right)^{2}}{n}}$\\ &=$\sqrt{\lambda^{2} \sigma_x^{2}}=|\lambda| \sigma_{x}=|\lambda| \sigma \end{aligned}$
